full_judgment:
8. Mr. M.H. Khondker, learned Counsel appearing for the appellants, submits that the learned Judges of the High Court division failed to notice that clause (a) of sub section (3) of section 96 of the Act, requires that application for pre-emption must be accompanied by a deposit of the entire consideration money of the property transferred or stated in the notice served under section 89, together with compensation @ 10 pc thereon, and She deposit being a condition precedent to the filing of the application, it cannot be entertained and its non-fulfillment renders the application liable to be dismissed; and that in the absence of any power to extend the time stipulated in the Act, the order is wholly illegal and without jurisdiction and cannot be sustained. The learned Counsel further submits that the pre-emptors were entitled to preempt the entire kabala land, but they having abandoned a portion of their claim in contravention of subsection (1) of section 96 of the Act. The direction given by the learned Judges of the High Court Division for depositing the balance of the consideration money with a view to converting the application to one for pre-emption of the entire kabala land is bad in law. With reference to subsection (1) of section 96 of the Act the learned Counsel submits that there is no scope for partial preemption, when a holding or a portion or a share oh holding is transferred. According to the learned Counsel even in the case of tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred may, within four months from the date of knowledge of such transfer, apply to the court for the holding or portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves; only restriction being no co-sharer tenant or tenants holding land contiguous to the land transferred shall have the right to purchase under this section unless he is a person to whom transfer to the holding or the portion or share thereof, as the case may be, can be made under sections 88 and 90 of the Act. This, as the learned Counsel submits, is necessary to avoid sub-division of holding. 

 19. On perusal of the other decisions cited by Mr. M.H Khandker namely, 17 D1 R 618, 10 DLR 659, 21 DLR 647, 22 DLR 61, 26 DIR .e3, 28 DLR (A.D.) 5, 38 CWN 288 and 38 CWN 654, and 43 CWN 200 it appears that none of the decisions has got any relevancy to the question under consideration. In all those cases the question of applicability of the rule of bar of partial preemption was considered either in a case of preemption under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act or in a case under the first part of section 96 of the Act. 

 20. The decision in the case of Sreemoti Monkhuhi Das Vs. Abdus Subhan Mean and others (1977) 29 DLR 195 cited by Mr. Ahmed Subhan in support of the proposition that the application for pre-emption of two plots transferred by a registered kabala is maintainable on the ground of having contiguity of land, appears to be relevant for our present consideration. In this case the pre-emptor filed an application for preemption under section 96 of the Act for preempting two plots out of three plots by the kabala on the ground that he has no land contiguous to the other plot. Preemption was allowed by the learned Munsif who held that in the facts of that case claim for pre-emption was not hit by the rule of partial preemption. On appeal the order of preemption was affirmed. In revision at the instance of the preemption under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the question was as to whether in an application for preemption by a tenant or tenants holding land "contiguous to the land transferred", the pre-emptor has been given the option to confine his claim to any part of the land transferred by the kabala. The learned single judge of the High Court after examining the language of different sub sections of section 96 of the Act did not accept the contention of the petitioner that a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred may preempt all or none. The learned Judge, with reference to the language of subsections (1)(2) and (5) b) of section 96 of the Act has correctly taken the view that the pre-emptor having been found to be a tenant holding land contiguous to only two plots out of three plots transferred, was entitled to preempt only the land to which he holds land contiguous thereto. 

 21. In the instant case we have noticed that the facts are simple. The pre-emptors having land contiguous to only two of the five plots transferred claimed preemption, and the case comes under the second part of sub-section (1) of section 96 of the Act. It has been already noticed that in case of preemption coming under the first part, the pre-emptor is required to establish his locus stands by showing that he is a co-sharer tenant of the holding. In such a case rule of partial pre-emption has been applied. In a case of preemption coming under the second part of sub-section (1) of section 96 of the act the tenant is not required to meet the same test. A tenant's right of preemption falling under the second part, the pre-emptor is required to establish that he has land contiguous to the land transferred. The expression holding land contiguous to the land transferred cannot be stretched to support the view that even in such a case the pre-emptor is required to include in the application for pre-emption also the lands to which he does not hold contiguous land and implead all the tenants holding contiguous lands to non-contiguous lands. This view cannot be reconciled with the different provisions of section 96 of the Act, as noticed above. 

 23. Before concluding the discussion regarding compliance of the requirement of sub-section (2) of section 96, we consider it necessary to make it clear that the view taken by us with regard to compliance of subsection (2) of section 96 is in accordance with the view taken by this court in the case of Matilal Sikd Jr V. Binodini Das, (1976) 28 DLR (Appellate Division) 5. It is the requirement of the statute that all the co-sharer tenants of the holding and all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred and the transferee shall be made parties, but a case of preemption under section 96 may not be defeated on the analogy of non-joinder of all co-sharers in a suit for partition. The reason is obvious, because, in a suit for partition non-joinder of a co-sharer may prove fatal to the suit, but the position in a preemption case is different. Right of preemption accrues on a transfer of a portion or share of a holding of a radiant or when a holding is transferred which gives rise to an application for preemption either under the first part or second part of sub-section (1) of section 96. This right is not absolute but subject to the right of other coherers and holders of land contiguous to the land transferred as the case may be. Requirement of the statute of impleading those in whose favour right of pre-emption accrued, is for the sole purpose of enabling the court to adjudicate the claim of all the parties having right to pre-empt according to the provision under sub-section (5) of section 9( in one proceeding and avoiding multiplicity of proceedings. So, for the sake of full am complete adjudication of the rights and gran ting relief there should not be absence of an, necessary party. 

 28. Further question for consideration is as to whether the direction given by the High Court Division for depositing the balance consideration money out of time is warranted by the law? Subsection (3) of section 96 of the Act requires that an application for preemption must be accompanied by deposit of the entire consideration money of the property transferred as stated in the notice under section 89 together with compensation @10% thereof. The statutory deposit being a condition precedent to the application being entertained, its noncompliance renders the application liable to be dismissed. The direction for depositing the balance consideration money out of time is also illegal and without jurisdiction.
